young.html: Michel de Montaigne was a French nobleman who, at 38, decided to stop working for the government and spend his days in a round stone tower on his family's land, with a thousand books. He painted wise sayings on the wooden beams of the ceiling. Then he started writing.

He didn't write stories or poems. He wrote down his thoughts about everything: friendship, fear, children, cats, sleep, cannibals, smells, how to die and how to live. He called each piece an essai, French for "a try," because he was trying out his thoughts. That is where our word essay comes from.
Montaigne liked to look at both sides of a question. He even had a medal made with a pair of balanced scales and the words Que sais-je?, "What do I know?"

young.name: gb-scales
young.cap: Put reasons on each side of the scales, the way Montaigne liked to weigh a question.

young.html: Write a real essay, Montaigne's way. Choose a small topic you know well: your dog, rainy days, your favorite food, being the youngest. Write one page that tries out your thoughts. Say what you think, then say what someone else might think, and end with a question you still have.
young.title: Try this: an essai

full.html: Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) grew up speaking Latin, because his father had him taught it from birth, and became a magistrate in Bordeaux. In 1563 his dearest friend, Étienne de La Boétie, died young. In 1571 Montaigne retired to his tower library and began writing short pieces that grew into the Essays: Books I and II in 1580, Book III in 1588, with additions in the margins until he died. In between, he traveled to Italy and served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux, during France's bitter wars of religion.

full.text: Reader, thou hast here an honest book; it doth at the outset forewarn thee that, in contriving the same, I have proposed to myself no other than a domestic and private end: I have had no consideration at all either to thy service or to my glory. ... for it is myself I paint. ... Thus, reader, myself am the matter of my book: there's no reason thou shouldst employ thy leisure about so frivolous and vain a subject. Therefore farewell.
full.author: Montaigne
full.tr: Charles Cotton, revised by William Carew Hazlitt

full.html: This was new. Writers before him had written about God, nature, history or the soul. Montaigne made his own changing, ordinary self the subject, not to boast but because, he said, each person bears the whole form of the human condition.

In "Of the Education of Children" he asks for a tutor "who has rather a well-made than a well-filled head," one who will make the pupil "examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads," so that what is learned becomes the student's own.

full.text: Bees cull their several sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but themselves afterward make the honey, which is all and purely their own, and no more thyme and marjoram ...

full.text: Doubt, and what it is good for

full.html: Montaigne's longest essay, the "Apology for Raymond Sebond," piles up examples of how weak human reason is: our senses deceive us, wise men disagree, and customs that seem natural in one country seem absurd in another. He wonders whether, when he plays with his cat, the cat is not amusing herself with him more than he with her. This kind of thinking is called skepticism: holding back from firm judgment when the reasons are unclear.

For Montaigne, doubt was not despair. It made him slow to condemn, tolerant of other people's customs, and wary of the certainty that drove the religious wars around him. He remained a Catholic all his life, and saw no conflict between doubting human reason and keeping his faith.

In "Of Cannibals" he writes about the native people of Brazil he had read about and met. He argues that Europeans call barbarous whatever is not their own custom, and that the cruelties of his own country's wars were no better. It is one of the first essays to turn the questions a traveler asks back on his own society.
Montaigne's method: try out a thought, look at the other side, give examples from books and from your own life, and admit what you don't know. That is still a good definition of an essay.
Thinking an essay has to be stiff and formal. Montaigne's essays wander, change their minds and talk to the reader. The five-paragraph essay of school is a later, tidier cousin.

deep.html: John Florio translated the Essays into English in 1603, and Shakespeare seems to have read him: Gonzalo's dream of an ideal commonwealth in The Tempest borrows lines from "Of Cannibals." Charles Cotton's translation (1685), revised by Hazlitt in 1877, is the one quoted here. Francis Bacon, later on this ladder, borrowed the word "essay" for his own, much shorter pieces (1597).

His early essays lean on the ancient Stoics, as in "That to Study Philosophy is to Learn to Die," which argues that thinking about death in advance robs it of its terror. His later essays, especially the last, "Of Experience," grow gentler: learn to live well, enjoy the body and the day, and know yourself. Readers like to watch his mind change across twenty years.

items: Is writing about yourself a way of learning about everyone?
When is doubt wise, and when does it become an excuse not to decide?
Are some customs truly better than others, or only different? How would you judge?
What is the difference between a full head and a well-made one?

deep.html: Pascal, on the next rung of this ladder, read Montaigne closely and argued with him, admiring his honesty and rejecting his ease with doubt. Descartes set out to defeat doubt with certainty.

questions: Montaigne said "What do I know?" What is something you are not sure about, even though people expect you to be?
If you wrote a book about yourself, what would be in the first chapter?
Montaigne compared a good student to a bee that makes its own honey. How can you make what you learn your own?
Is it fair to judge people from other places by our own customs? When might it be right to?
Montaigne's best friend died young, and he wrote about friendship for the rest of his life. What makes a friendship last?
